name: Git Basics
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Track changes with commits, branches, merges and remotes, and undo mistakes without losing work.

lesson.intro: Git records snapshots of a project so you can see what changed, try ideas in parallel, and go back when something breaks. This lesson covers the everyday loop of staging and committing, then branches, merges, remotes, and how to undo mistakes safely.

sections.title: Working tree, staging area, commits
sections.body:
Your changes live in three places. The working tree is the files you edit. The staging area (also called the index) is a draft of your next commit. The repository holds the commits: saved snapshots, each with an author, a message and a link to the commit before it.

- `git add file` copies the current version of a file into the staging area.
- `git commit -m "message"` saves everything staged as one new commit.
- `git status` shows what is untracked, modified, or staged.
- `git diff` shows edits you have not staged yet; `git diff --staged` shows what the next commit will contain.
- `git log --oneline` lists commits, newest first, one per line.

`git add` stores a snapshot of the file at that moment. If you edit the file again afterwards, the new edit is not staged until you run `git add` again. `git status --short` shows this as `MM`: the first column is the staging area and the second is the working tree.
sections.code:
git status --short
?? notes.txt          # untracked: Git has never seen it
git add notes.txt
git status --short
A  notes.txt          # staged as a new file
git commit -m "Add notes"
git log --oneline
705cb9f Add notes
sections.tip: `git commit -am "msg"` stages and commits modified tracked files in one step, but it never picks up new, untracked files.

check.question: You run `git add app.js`, edit app.js again, then run `git commit`. What goes into the commit?
choices: app.js as it was when you ran git add
app.js with the newest edit included
Nothing, because app.js changed after staging
Two commits, one for each version
check.explanation: git add stores a snapshot of the file at that moment. The later edit stays in the working tree, unstaged, until you add it again.

sections.title: Branches and switching
sections.body:
A branch is a name that points at one commit. It is not a copy of your files, which is why creating one is instant. When you commit, the branch you are on moves forward to the new commit; every other branch stays where it was.

`HEAD` is how Git knows which branch you are on. `git branch` lists branches and marks the current one with `*`.

- `git switch -c name` creates a branch at the current commit and switches to it. Older guides write this as `git checkout -b name`.
- `git switch name` moves to an existing branch. Git rewrites the files in your working tree to match that branch's latest commit.
- `git branch name` only creates the branch. You stay where you were.

If you have uncommitted edits, Git carries them along when you switch, unless they would be overwritten by the other branch. In that case it refuses to switch, so commit your work first.
sections.code:
git switch -c login-form     # create a branch and move onto it
git branch
* login-form
  main
# edit, add and commit on login-form ...
git switch main              # files go back to how main has them
sections.tip: Make a branch for each separate piece of work. Branches are cheap, and they keep half-finished ideas off main.

check.question: You are on `main` and run `git switch -c experiment`, then make two commits. Where does `main` point now?
choices: At the newest commit on experiment
At the first of the two new commits
At the same commit as before you branched
Nowhere, because main was renamed to experiment
check.explanation: Only the branch you are on moves when you commit. main still points at the commit where experiment started.

sections.title: Merging and conflicts
sections.body:
`git merge other` brings the commits from `other` into the branch you are on. There are two outcomes:

- Fast-forward: your branch has no new commits since `other` split off, so Git simply moves your branch pointer forward. No new commit is made.
- Merge commit: both branches have new commits, so Git combines them in a new commit that has two parents.

If both branches changed the same lines of a file, Git cannot choose for you. It stops with a conflict and writes both versions into the file between markers. The part between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your current branch; the part between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the branch being merged in.

To resolve it, edit the file to the final content you want and delete the markers. Then `git add` the file to mark it resolved and `git commit` to finish the merge. If you would rather start over, `git merge --abort` puts everything back to how it was before the merge.
sections.code:
git merge fix
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in notes.txt
cat notes.txt
<<<<<<< HEAD
title: Release
=======
title: Final
>>>>>>> fix
sections.tip: During a conflict, `git status` lists the unmerged files under "both modified".

check.question: In a conflict block, which lines come from the branch you are currently on?
choices: The lines between ======= and >>>>>>>
The lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======
The lines after the >>>>>>> marker
Neither; Git keeps your version in a backup file
check.explanation: HEAD is your current branch, so its version sits right after the <<<<<<< HEAD marker. The incoming branch's version follows the ======= line.

sections.title: Remotes: clone, fetch, pull, push
sections.body:
A remote is another copy of the repository, usually on a server such as GitHub. `git clone URL` downloads the whole history and names that remote `origin`.

Git keeps remote-tracking branches like `origin/main` to remember what the remote looked like the last time you talked to it.

- `git fetch` downloads new commits and updates `origin/main`. It does not touch your own branches or your files.
- `git pull` is a fetch followed by merging the remote branch into your current branch.
- `git push` uploads your commits. The first push of a new branch is usually `git push -u origin name`, which also sets it as the upstream so later a plain `git push` or `git pull` knows where to go.

If someone else pushed first, your push is rejected, because it would throw their commits away. Pull, fix any conflicts, then push again.
sections.code:
git clone https://github.com/example/app.git
cd app
git fetch       # update origin/main, leave my work alone
git status      # Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 1 commit
git pull        # fetch, then merge origin/main into main
git push        # send my new commits to origin
sections.tip: Avoid `git push --force` on shared branches. It replaces the remote branch with yours and can delete other people's commits.

check.question: After `git fetch`, which of these has changed?
choices: Your local main branch and its commits
The files in your working tree
The staging area for your next commit
The remote-tracking branch origin/main
check.explanation: fetch only downloads commits and updates remote-tracking branches such as origin/main. Your branches, files and staging area are untouched until you merge or pull.

sections.title: Undoing mistakes and ignoring files
sections.body:
Pick the undo tool by where the mistake is:

- `git restore file` throws away unstaged edits in the working tree. Git cannot bring them back, so be sure.
- `git restore --staged file` unstages a file and keeps your edits in the working tree.
- `git revert <commit>` adds a new commit that does the opposite of an old one. History is kept, so it is safe on branches others have pulled.
- `git reset <commit>` moves the current branch back to an older commit, rewriting history. `--soft` keeps the undone changes staged, the default `--mixed` keeps them as unstaged edits, and `--hard` deletes them.

Rule of thumb: revert commits that have been pushed; reset only commits that exist on your machine alone.

A `.gitignore` file lists patterns for files Git should leave alone, such as `*.log`, `build/` or `.env`. It only affects untracked files. If a file is already tracked, adding it to `.gitignore` changes nothing until you run `git rm --cached file`, which stops tracking it but leaves it on disk.
sections.code:
git restore --staged app.js   # unstage, keep the edits
git restore app.js            # discard edits in the working tree
git revert HEAD               # new commit that undoes the last one
git reset --soft HEAD~1       # drop the last commit, keep its changes staged

# .gitignore
*.log
build/
.env
sections.tip: Lost a commit after `git reset --hard`? `git reflog` lists every commit HEAD has pointed to, so you can usually find it again.

check.question: Which command throws away your unstaged edits to app.js, with no way to get them back from Git?
choices: git restore --staged app.js
git revert app.js
git restore app.js
git reset --soft HEAD~1
check.explanation: git restore with no options copies the staged (or committed) version over your working file, so unstaged edits are lost. With --staged it only unstages and keeps the edits.

keyTerms.definition: The files on disk that you edit, which may differ from the last commit.
Also called the index: the snapshot that the next git commit will save.
A saved snapshot of the staged files with an author, a message and a link to its parent commit.
A movable name that points at a commit and moves forward when you commit on it.
The pointer to the branch (and so the commit) you currently have checked out.
A merge where Git only moves the branch pointer forward because the current branch has no new commits.
A stop during a merge when both branches changed the same lines, so you must choose the final content.
Another copy of the repository, such as origin on GitHub, that you fetch from and push to.

summary: `git add` snapshots a file into the staging area; `git commit` saves everything staged as one commit.
A branch is a movable name for a commit; committing moves only the branch you are on.
Merges fast-forward when they can; a conflict means both sides changed the same lines, so fix the file, add it, and commit.
`fetch` downloads without touching your work, `pull` is fetch plus merge, and `push` is rejected until you have the remote's commits.
Revert pushed commits, reset only local ones, and remember `.gitignore` only affects untracked files.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never used Git what happens between editing a file and having that change on GitHub, using the words working tree, staging area, commit and push.

questions.question: Running `git status --short` prints `MM app.js`. What does that mean?
choices: app.js was modified on two different branches at once
app.js has a merge conflict that still needs fixing
A version is staged, and newer edits are not staged
app.js was moved to a new folder and then modified
questions.explanation: The first column describes the staging area and the second the working tree. M in both means you staged a version and then edited the file again. A merge conflict shows as UU, not MM.

questions.question: Type the command that shows the changes you have already staged, that is, what the next commit will contain.
questions.explanation: Plain git diff compares the working tree with the staging area, so it shows only unstaged edits. git diff --staged (same as --cached) compares the staging area with the last commit.

questions.question: You edit the tracked file app.js and create a new file notes.md, then run `git commit -am "Update"`. What happens?
choices: app.js is committed; notes.md stays untracked
Both files are committed
Nothing is committed because notes.md is untracked
notes.md is committed; app.js stays modified
questions.explanation: The -a flag stages changes to files Git already tracks. It never adds new files, so notes.md stays untracked until you git add it.

questions.question: You have no uncommitted changes and run `git switch feature`. What happens to the files in your working tree?
choices: They stay exactly as they were on the previous branch
They change to match the latest commit on feature
They are emptied until you run git pull
Only files you staged earlier are updated
questions.explanation: Switching branches moves HEAD and rewrites the working tree to match the commit that branch points to. Switching back restores the other version.

questions.question: Type one command that creates a branch named `login` and switches to it.
questions.explanation: git switch -c creates the branch and moves onto it in one step. git branch login would only create it, leaving you on the old branch.

questions.question: The developer wanted this fix on a new branch, but it ended up on main. What went wrong?
questions.code:
git branch hotfix
# edit app.js
git commit -am "Fix crash"
git log --oneline -1    # the fix is on main
choices: git commit -am always commits to main
hotfix has to be pushed before anyone can commit to it
A branch cannot be created before the files are edited
git branch only creates hotfix; it never switched to it
questions.explanation: git branch hotfix creates the branch but leaves you on main, so the commit moved main. Use git switch -c hotfix, or git switch hotfix after creating it.

questions.question: You are on main, and main has no new commits since feature branched off it. What does `git merge feature` do?
choices: Creates a merge commit with two parents
Copies the feature commits onto main as new commits
Moves main forward to the latest commit on feature
Deletes the feature branch after merging it
questions.explanation: Because main has nothing new, Git can fast-forward: it just moves the main pointer to feature's latest commit. A merge commit is only needed when both branches have new commits.

questions.question: You fixed the conflict in notes.txt and removed the markers. Complete the step that tells Git the conflict is resolved.
questions.code:
git merge fix
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in notes.txt
# ... edit notes.txt and remove the markers ...
_____
git commit
choices: git resolve notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git restore notes.txt
git merge notes.txt
questions.explanation: Staging the file marks it resolved; git status changes it from UU to M. Then git commit creates the merge commit. There is no git resolve command, and restore would not mark anything resolved.

questions.question: A merge stops with a conflict in config.yml. Which situation caused it?
choices: Both branches edited config.yml, but in far-apart sections
Only the branch being merged in changed config.yml
Both branches made the identical change to config.yml
Both branches changed the same lines of config.yml
questions.explanation: Git merges changes automatically when they touch different parts of a file, or when only one side changed it, or when both made the same change. It stops only when the two sides changed the same lines differently.

questions.question: A merge hit conflicts and you want to go back to exactly how things were before you started it. Type the command.
questions.explanation: git merge --abort stops the merge and restores the branch and files to their state before git merge ran.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
choices: fetch only downloads; pull downloads and merges into your branch
fetch is for new clones; pull is for existing repositories
fetch uploads your commits; pull downloads other people's
There is none; pull is just another name for fetch
questions.explanation: fetch updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main and stops there. pull runs a fetch and then merges the remote branch into your current branch, which can change your files.

questions.question: Why was this push rejected?
questions.code:
git push
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'origin'
choices: You forgot to run git add before pushing
Your branch has no commits to push yet
The remote has commits you do not have; pull them, then push
Pushing to main is never allowed; push to a new branch
questions.explanation: Someone pushed to main after you last pulled. Git refuses because accepting your push would discard their commits. git pull brings them in; then your push works. Forcing the push would delete their work.

questions.question: Complete the command that pushes the new local branch feature to origin for the first time and sets it as the upstream, so a plain `git push` works later.
choices: -f
-u
--all
-d
questions.explanation: -u (short for --set-upstream) pushes and records origin/feature as the branch's upstream. -f force-overwrites the remote branch and -d deletes it.

questions.question: You ran `git add secrets.txt` by mistake. Type the command that unstages it and leaves the file itself unchanged.
questions.explanation: git restore --staged removes the file from the staging area and keeps your working copy. Plain git restore secrets.txt would do something different: overwrite the working copy.

questions.question: You run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. Where are the changes from the commit you undid?
choices: In the working tree, but unstaged
Gone, deleted along with the commit
Moved to a new branch named HEAD~1
Still staged, ready to commit again
questions.explanation: --soft only moves the branch pointer back, so the undone changes stay staged. The default --mixed would leave them unstaged, and --hard would delete them.

questions.question: Complete the .gitignore line so every file ending in .log is ignored, in every folder of the project.
choices: *.log
/*.log
*.log/
logs/
questions.explanation: A pattern with no slash matches at any depth, so *.log ignores app.log and src/debug.log alike. A leading slash anchors it to the top folder only, and a trailing slash matches only directories.

questions.question: When would you undo a commit with `git revert` rather than `git reset`, and why?
questions.answer: Use revert when the commit is already pushed or shared. It adds a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody's history is rewritten. Reset moves the branch back and rewrites history, so it is only safe for commits that exist on your machine alone.
questions.explanation: Rewriting commits that others already have forces them to untangle diverged histories. A revert is an ordinary new commit, so everyone can simply pull it.
